title: Scope and Sequence
text:
How This Course Is Organized
This is a spiral course, not a sequence of topic units. Students do not spend weeks on output, then weeks on input, then weeks on decisions. From the first week, they read real programs that already use output, input, variables, decisions, loops, strings, and lists. Each module comes back to all of these ideas at a deeper level.

Modules are built around themes and anchor programs, not single programming constructs. Each module has a purpose students can see (find out about this computer, check whether it meets a need, build a game, send a secret message, investigate data).
Reading makes early depth possible. Students can read and predict code that uses a loop or a list weeks before they are asked to write one. When code uses something not yet taught, the teacher explains it briefly and moves on: “You’ll learn to write these properly later.”
Each idea moves through four levels across the course: read it, modify it, write it, then design with it.
Not project-based. Lessons stay teacher-led and structured (see the teaching approach); a full independent project comes only at the end.

title: Scope and Sequence
text:
Modules

Module 1 — About This Computer (15 h)
Purpose: Ask the computer about itself.
Anchor programs: a two-line program that prints the CPU type (platform.machine()); a labelled computer report built from the platform module; a report that stores answers in variables; later, a version that asks the user’s name and greets them with a hardware summary, and one that loops through a list of facts.
Pacing: one library first. Lessons 1–2 use only platform, starting from a single line. Other modules (os for cores, shutil for storage) wait until Module 2.

Taught explicitly: what a program is; reading and predicting output; import and calling a module’s functions; print() and f-strings; variables; tracing line by line; finding tools with dir() and the documentation; comments and naming conventions; syntax and run-time errors and how to read them
Met through reading: input(), a simple if, a for loop over a list
Computer science: CPU types (arm64, x86_64) and operating systems; where code runs: the classroom computer, a virtual computer in the browser, and a cloud server (Google Colab); where variables live (RAM) and where arithmetic happens (CPU); source code vs. machine code; interpreters vs. compilers; the parts of the programming environment; organizing program files

Expectations: A1.1, A2.1, A2.2, A3.1, A4.2, A4.3, A4.4, C1.1, C1.4, C2.1, C3.1, C3.3, C3.4, C3.5


Module 2 — Spec Checker (17 h)
Purpose: Decide whether a computer meets a user’s needs.
Anchor programs: a storage calculator (bytes to gigabytes, percentage used); a “will this game run?” checker comparing a computer’s specifications to requirements; a computer recommender for different users.

New modules, one at a time: os.cpu_count() for cores, then shutil.disk_usage() for storage
Taught explicitly: input and type conversion; data types; arithmetic, integer division, remainder, order of operations; comparison and logical operators; if/elif/else; handling bad input with try/except; user-friendly prompts and messages; test plans with normal and boundary cases
Revisited and extended: output formatting, variables, reading error messages
Met through modifying: a loop that checks a list of requirements; string methods for cleaning input (.strip(), .lower())
Computer science: internal components and peripherals and their specifications; relating specifications to user requirements; the input-process-output model

Expectations: A1.1, A1.3, A1.4, A2.1, A2.2, A4.1, A4.3, A4.5, B1.1, B1.3, B2.5, B3.2, B3.3, B4.4, C1.1, C1.2, C1.3


Module 3 — Games of Chance (17 h)
Purpose: Build games and simulations with randomness.
Anchor programs: dice rolling and a simulation of 1000 rolls; a number-guessing game; rock-paper-scissors against the computer; a “lucky prime” challenge.

Taught explicitly: while loops (game loops, input validation); for loops and range(); counters and accumulators; nested loops and decisions; the random module; writing first simple functions; flow charts and pseudocode; debugging by tracing and printing variables
Revisited and extended: decisions, input validation, test plans, formatted output
Met through modifying: lists of choices; strings in game messages
Computer science: problem-solving strategies; designing from a program skeleton; determining primes

Expectations: A2.2, A2.3, A3.1, A3.2, A4.1, A4.4, B1.1, B2.1, B2.4, B3.2, B4.5


Module 4 — Secret Messages (17 h)
Purpose: Hide and reveal messages, and learn how computers store text.
Anchor programs: a binary and hexadecimal converter; a program that shows the Unicode value of every character in a message; a Caesar cipher that encodes and decodes; a password strength checker.

Taught explicitly: strings as sequences (indexing, slicing, traversal, methods); ord() and chr(); writing functions with parameters and return values; local and global scope; reusable modules
Revisited and extended: loops, decisions, input validation, debugging
Met through modifying: lists of words and characters
Computer science: binary, hexadecimal, ASCII, and Unicode; cryptography as a research area; malware and a system protection plan; backing up and archiving files

Expectations: A1.2, A3.1, A3.2, A4.1, B1.1, B2.3, C2.2, C2.3, D2.1


Module 5 — Data Detective (18 h)
Purpose: Investigate real data about computers and the environment.
Anchor programs: an analysis of device power use and e-waste data; a class survey analyzer; a sorted leaderboard that accepts new scores and removes old ones.

Taught explicitly: lists as one-dimensional arrays (elements, indexes, bounds); creating, modifying, and accessing lists; count, total, highest and lowest value, linear search; inserting into a sorted list and deleting from the middle; breaking a program into functions; structure charts; describing and comparing program designs
Revisited and extended: functions and scope, loops, strings, testing with a full range of cases
Computer science: environmental and health effects of computer use; reducing the impact of computers; using computers to protect the environment; recycling and community partners

Expectations: A1.5, A1.6, A2.3, A3.2, A4.4, A4.5, B2.2, B2.3, B2.4, B3.1, D1.1, D1.2, D1.3, D1.4


Module 6 — Software Development Project (20 h)
Purpose: Plan, build, test, and present a program of the student’s own design.

Taught explicitly: phases, milestones, and products of the software development life cycle; clarifying a specification (dialogue, questionnaires, research); Gantt charts and milestones in a teacher-led project; written status reports
Design level: students choose and combine every idea from the spiral
Working practices: working independently with documentation and as part of a team; test plans; debugging; professional code conventions

Expectations: A4.2, A4.5, B1.2, B2.1, B2.2, B2.3, B2.4, B2.5, B4.1, B4.2, B4.3, B4.4, B4.5, B4.6, C3.2


Computer Science in the World (6 h, alongside Modules 2–5)
Purpose: See where computer science leads.
Short lessons placed between modules, with an independent research report submitted in stages:

Emerging research areas (e.g., artificial intelligence, cryptography, computer vision) and collaborative research with other fields
Research report on an area of computer science, in a format of the student’s choice
Careers, trends, experiential learning, postsecondary programs, and supports for non-traditional career choices
Essential Skills and work habits (Ontario Skills Passport)

Expectations: D2.1, D2.2, D2.3, D3.1, D3.2, D3.3, D3.4, D3.5

title: Scope and Sequence
text:
Assessment Overview
Following Ontario’s Growing Success policy: 70% of the final grade comes from evaluations during the course and 30% from final evaluations.

Every lesson: an exit ticket, usually a code-reading or tracing question (assessment for and as learning, not counted toward the grade).
Within each module: short quizzes, and a few small programs built from the anchor programs.
End of Modules 1–5: a module test that always includes a code-reading and tracing section. Because the course spirals, every test may include earlier ideas.
Computer Science in the World: the staged research report.
Final 30%: the Module 6 software development project and a final exam that includes code reading and tracing.

title: Scope and Sequence
text:
Python Notes for Teachers
The 2008 curriculum uses general terms. In Python:

Constants (A1.1) are a naming convention (UPPER_CASE); Python does not enforce them.
One-dimensional arrays (A1.5, A1.6) are taught as Python lists, used with a single data type and fixed purpose.
Procedures (A3.2) are functions that do not return a value.
Compiler error messages (A4.3) appear in Python as tracebacks; C3.4 contrasts Python’s interpreter with compiled languages such as C or Java.
Hardware programs use only the standard library (platform, then os and shutil). Results depend on where the code runs: macOS reports itself as “Darwin”; the course website’s runnable code reports a browser virtual computer (wasm32, Emscripten); Google Colab reports a Google cloud server (typically x86_64, Linux). These differences are a deliberate teaching point. Use platform.machine() for the CPU type; platform.processor() is unreliable across systems. Total RAM is not available from the standard library.

title: Scope and Sequence
text:
Teaching Approach
Every lesson follows the course’s reading-first approach: students read, trace, and predict code before they write it. Each lesson moves through review, a teacher-led worked example, then Predict, Run, Investigate, Modify, and Make (PRIMM). Writing new code from scratch always comes after reading and modifying.

title: Lesson 2: Exploring the platform Library

At a Glance

Big idea: a module is a toolbox you can explore, and variables let a program remember answers to use later.
Students will: list the platform toolbox with dir(), look up a function in the documentation, trace a program that stores answers in variables, and read two common error messages.
Students make: a computer report built from four platform functions stored in variables.
Prepare: run l02_report_variables.py and both mistake programs, so you’ve seen the error messages students will see.
After class: Lesson 2 practice, then the Module 1 Assignment.
Where it fits: builds on Lesson 1; part of Module 1.

title: Lesson 2: Exploring the platform Library
text:
Learning Goals

Find out what tools a module contains, using dir() and the Python documentation.
Store answers in variables and use them later in a program.
Trace which variables exist and what they hold, line by line.
Read two common error messages and explain what caused them.

title: Lesson 2: Exploring the platform Library
text:
Success Criteria
Students can say:

I can find a new function in the platform module and use it.
I can predict the output of a program that stores values in variables.
I can explain what an AttributeError message is telling me.

title: Lesson 2: Exploring the platform Library
section: Teach: What Else Is in the Toolbox? (15 min)
text:
Teach: What Else Is in the Toolbox? (15 min)
A module can contain many tools. dir() lists them. Run it and read the list together.












TipTeacher prompt



Think aloud while reading the list:

“Names starting with an underscore, like _comparable_version, are for Python’s own use. We skip those.”
“Some names look familiar from Lesson 1: machine, system, node, python_version, release.”
“Others are new: platform, architecture, version, uname. The name gives a hint, but the documentation tells us for sure.”



Open the official documentation for the module: docs.python.org/3/library/platform.html. Find platform.machine() and read its description together. Then choose one new function from the list, predict what it does from its name, and try it.

title: Lesson 2: Exploring the platform Library
text:
Predict, Then Step (15 min)
This is Lesson 1’s computer report, rewritten so that each answer is stored in a variable before it is printed. Read it without running it, then answer:

Which lines ask the computer a question? Which lines print?
What will the first line of output be?
How is this program different from Lesson 1’s program? Will the output be different?

Type your prediction in the box, then press Step to run one line at a time. Watch the Variables panel as well as the output.






TipTeacher prompt: the Variables panel (first use)




“Same colours as last lesson: yellow with an arrow is the next line, green just ran.”
“There’s a new panel today: Variables. A variable is a name that holds a value. When line 3 runs, watch a new row appear.”
After stepping line 3: “Nothing was printed, but something happened. The answer was stored under the name cpu.”
“The quotation marks around 'wasm32' tell us the value is text. Python calls text a string. The quotation marks won’t be printed.”



import platform

cpu = platform.machine()
system = platform.system()
name = platform.node()

print("Computer report for", name)
print("CPU type:", cpu)
print("Operating system:", system)

What the variables hold

After line 3 runs, which variable exists and what is its value?
Lines 3–5 run, but nothing is printed yet. Where did the answers go?
Line 7 uses name, which was created on line 5. What would happen if line 7 came before line 5?

Spot the problem
Each program has a mistake. Predict what will happen, then step through it and read the result carefully.






TipTeacher prompt: reading an error (first use)



After Program B stops:

“A red line means Python stopped on that line because of an error. The lines below it never ran.”
“The message under the buttons has three parts: the line number, the kind of error (AttributeError), and a description in plain words. Read them in that order.”
“Errors aren’t failures. They’re Python telling us exactly where to look.”



Program A
import platform

print(platform.machine)
Program B
import platform

print(platform.cpu())

Program A does not crash, but prints something strange. What is missing?
Program B stops with an AttributeError. Which line caused it? What is the message telling you?
How could dir(platform) have prevented the mistake in Program B?
Run Program B on the classroom computer. How does the full error message there show the same information?

title: Lesson 2: Exploring the platform Library
text:
Teacher Notes

Variables. A variable is a name that stores a value. cpu = platform.machine() asks the question once and keeps the answer, so the program can use it later, as many times as needed.
Step-through box. It runs the real program in the browser, so platform works and the variables hold the browser’s answers ('wasm32', 'Emscripten'). Python Tutor is not used here because it does not allow the platform module.
Changing a variable (e.g. system = "macOS" after system = "Darwin") is not part of this lesson; it comes when programs start calculating with stored values.
dir() output is long and includes names starting with _; tell students to skip those. In the browser and on the classroom computer, the lists may differ slightly between Python versions.
Spot the problem. Without parentheses, platform.machine is the tool itself, not its answer, so Python prints a description of the function, e.g. <function machine at 0x104cb3e20>. The AttributeError says the module has no tool by that name. The step-through box highlights the line that caused the error and shows the error type and message; Thonny, IDLE, and VS Code show the same information as a full traceback, which students should learn to read too.
Spiral. Students now write variables and read error messages. Calculating with values (os.cpu_count(), storage in gigabytes) comes in Module 2.
Answers are in the private teacher files.

title: Lesson 1: Ask the Computer About Itself
text:
At a Glance

Big idea: a program can ask the computer about itself, and the answer depends on which computer runs it.
Students will: guess their computer’s processor and operating system, read and step through a four-line program that checks, then change it.
Students make: a short report program that prints the operating system and its version.
Prepare: run l01_computer_report.py on your computer and on a student computer; optionally in Colab for the demonstration.
After class: Lesson 1 practice.
Where it fits: the first lesson of Module 1. Lesson 2 adds dir(), variables, and error messages.

title: Lesson 1: Ask the Computer About Itself
text:
Learning Goals

Read a short Python program and predict what it will print.
Explain what import platform and print() do.
Explain what a CPU type such as arm64 or x86_64 tells us.
Recognize that a program reports on whatever computer it actually runs on.

title: Lesson 1: Ask the Computer About Itself
text:
Success Criteria
Students can say:

I can predict which parts of a program’s output are fixed text and which parts come from the computer.
I can name the CPU type and operating system of the computer I am using.
I can explain why the same program gives different answers in different places.

title: Lesson 1: Ask the Computer About Itself
text:
Warm-up (5 min)
Students write down their best guesses about the computer in front of them:

What kind of processor (CPU) does it have?
Which operating system does it run?
What is the computer’s name?

Keep the guesses. Today’s programs will check them.

title: Lesson 1: Ask the Computer About Itself
section: Teach: Two Lines of Python (15 min)
text:
Teach: Two Lines of Python (15 min)
Show this program and read it aloud before running it.
import platform

print(platform.machine())






TipTeacher prompt



Think aloud while reading, one line at a time:

“import platform brings in a module: a toolbox of ready-made code that comes with Python. This one can answer questions about the computer.”
“platform.machine() asks one question: what type of CPU is this? The dot means ‘the machine tool from the platform toolbox’. The parentheses mean ‘use it now’.”
“print() shows the answer on the screen.”
“Python runs a program from top to bottom, one line at a time.”



Now run it on the classroom computer (Thonny, IDLE, or VS Code). Compare the answer with the warm-up guesses.
What the answer means. The CPU type names the family of processor and the instructions it understands:








Answer
Meaning
Found in




arm64 or aarch64
64-bit ARM processor
Apple silicon Macs, most phones and tablets, some Chromebooks and Windows laptops


x86_64 or AMD64
64-bit Intel or AMD processor
Most Windows laptops and desktops, older Macs, most servers



Windows reports Intel and AMD processors as AMD64 because AMD designed the 64-bit version of this processor family.

title: Lesson 1: Ask the Computer About Itself
text:
Predict, Then Run (15 min)
Read this program without running it, then answer:

How many lines will it print?
Which words will appear exactly as they are written in the code?
Which parts will depend on the computer?

Type your prediction in the box. Then press Step to run the program one line at a time, and compare each line of output with your prediction.






TipTeacher prompt: the step-through box (first use)



Before anyone presses Step, explain the colours:

“This box runs the program one line at a time. Nothing has run yet.”
“The red arrow on a yellow line marks the next line Python will run. It hasn’t run yet.”
“When I press Step, that line runs and turns green. Green means just ran. The arrow moves to the next line.”
“Anything the program prints appears in the Output box the moment its line turns green. Your prediction stays above it, so you can compare.”
“Back replays a step. Run all jumps to the end. Start over resets everything.”

Then: “Write your prediction first. No pressing Step until you’ve committed.”


import platform

print("CPU type:", platform.machine())
print("Operating system:", platform.system())
print("Computer name:", platform.node())
Now run the same program on the classroom computer (Thonny, IDLE, or VS Code). Which lines of output are the same as on this page? Which are different?

title: Lesson 1: Ask the Computer About Itself
text:
Teacher Notes

Why platform only. Every platform function follows one pattern (platform.something() gives back text), is safe to experiment with, and answers a question students care about. Other modules (os for cores, shutil for storage) come later, one at a time.
machine(), not processor(). platform.processor() is unreliable: it returns a long description on Windows, arm on Apple silicon, and often nothing on Linux or in the browser.
Three places, three computers.

Classroom computer: the real hardware, e.g. arm64 / Darwin (macOS) or AMD64 / Windows. macOS reports itself as “Darwin”, the name of its core.
This web page: Python runs inside the browser (Pyodide, WebAssembly). It reports wasm32, Emscripten, and emscripten: a small virtual computer that exists only inside the browser tab, though it still uses the classroom computer’s processor underneath.
Google Colab: the code runs on a Google server in a data centre. It typically reports x86_64, Linux, and a random-looking machine name. Check by running the program in Colab before class.

Colab access. Many school boards disable Colab for student accounts, so plan it as a teacher demonstration. For setting up classroom computers, see Before You Begin.
Predict, then run. The step-through box keeps the prediction next to the real output. Encourage students to commit to a prediction before pressing Step; the Back button lets them replay any line.
First load. The step-through box and the runnable boxes download Python into the browser the first time (about 10 MB), which can take a few seconds.
Spiral. Students meet import, function calls, and comma-separated print() items through reading today. Variables come in Lesson 2.
Answers are in the private teacher files.

title: Before You Begin
text:
Expectations: C3.1 (software development environment), D1.4 (organizations that refurbish computers)
This course asks the computer about itself. The first program students read reports the CPU type, the operating system, and the computer’s name. Module 2 adds the number of CPU cores and the free disk space, and later modules may look at the network. All of this only means something when the code runs on the computer in front of the student.
Get Python working before Lesson 1, both on your own demonstration computer and on the computers your students will use.

title: Before You Begin
text:
Your Demonstration Computer
You will model nearly every lesson: reading code aloud, predicting, running it, and stepping through mistakes. For this you need a computer that:

has Python 3 installed locally, not just a browser tab;
has an editor students will also use. Thonny is the best first choice for beginners because its debugger steps through code one line at a time. IDLE (included with Python) also works;
connects to the projector, with the editor’s font large enough to read from the back of the room;
has already run each lesson’s example programs. Run them the day before, so you know what this computer will report.

Don’t count on a board-imaged laptop letting you install software on the day. Ask IT early.

For you: VS Code and agentic programming
Install VS Code as well, and learn to use it. It’s the editor many professional developers use, and it’s where agentic programming happens: AI coding agents (such as GitHub Copilot, Claude Code, and Codex) work inside the editor. They read your project, write and change code, run it, and explain what they did.
Every teacher, and especially every CS teacher, should learn to work this way. It’s quickly becoming how software gets built. Knowing it firsthand helps you prepare examples faster and answer students’ questions about AI honestly. It also prepares you for the world your students are heading into. GitHub Copilot is free for verified teachers through GitHub Education.
Students start in Thonny, where they read and trace every line themselves. VS Code is a natural next step once they’re comfortable, and a good place to show how AI tools change (and don’t change) the need to read code carefully.

title: Before You Begin
text:
Student Computers
Students need a place to run, change, break, and fix programs every day, not only to read them. In order of preference:

1. Real computers with Python installed
The best choice. Lab or classroom computers with Python and an editor installed give the real experience: real hardware, real files, and a real operating system to explore.


2. Refurbished computers
Strongly recommended if your school doesn’t have enough computers. Older desktops and laptops are cheap and run Python perfectly well.

In Canada, the federal Computers for Schools Plus program supplies refurbished computers to schools. In Ontario it’s run by Renewed Computer Technology. Schools can order through Computers for Schools Ontario.
Many older computers can’t run Windows 11, and Windows 10 stopped receiving security updates in October 2025. A free Linux system (for example, Ubuntu or Linux Mint) runs well on older hardware and comes with Python already installed.
A room with a mix of Windows, macOS, and Linux computers is a bonus. Each one gives different answers to the same program, which is exactly what Lesson 1 investigates.
Refurbishing ties into the curriculum: expectation D1.4 names “private companies that refurbish computers” as an example.



3. Raspberry Pi and other small computers
A Raspberry Pi is a small, inexpensive computer. Raspberry Pi OS comes with Python 3 and Thonny already installed. Each one needs a power supply, a microSD card, and a monitor, keyboard, and mouse (classroom monitors often work). Its ARM processor reports something different again (on the 64-bit system, aarch64 and Linux), which makes for a good comparison. Other small or portable computers that can install Python work too.






TipChromebooks



If your board allows it, a Chromebook’s Linux development environment can install Python and Thonny. The code runs inside a Linux container, so it reports Linux rather than ChromeOS. That’s a good discussion point, but it isn’t the same as a computer running Python directly.

title: Before You Begin
section: Online Options: Fine in a Pinch
text:
Online Options: Fine in a Pinch
Browser-based Python is useful when a computer can’t install anything, for homework, or as a backup on a day the lab is down:

The runnable boxes on this site. These need nothing installed. Python runs inside the browser tab.
Google Colab. These are notebooks that run on Google’s servers. Many school boards turn Colab off for student accounts, so check before you plan around it.
Callysto Hub. These are free Jupyter notebooks for Canadian classrooms, hosted on Canadian servers. Cybera and PIMS wound down their involvement in Callysto in 2024, and the resources remain available. Confirm that sign-in works for your students before relying on it.

None of these gives students the experience this course is built around. The code doesn’t run on the student’s computer, so the hardware questions get answers about a different machine:








Where the code runs
What platform describes
Typical CPU / operating system




Classroom computer
The computer in front of the student
AMD64 / Windows, arm64 / Darwin, x86_64 / Linux


This site’s runnable boxes
A small virtual computer inside the browser tab
wasm32 / Emscripten


Colab or Callysto
A server in a data centre somewhere else
Usually x86_64 / Linux



Online notebooks also can’t see the student’s own files, drives, or classroom network. Lesson 1 uses these differences on purpose, as a comparison. They make a poor only option.

text:
This course is built to address every expectation in Ontario’s ICS3U course (Grade 11 Introduction to Computer Science, University Preparation, 2008 curriculum), and every lesson is tagged with the expectations it covers.

title: About This Course
text:
This course is built to address every expectation in Ontario’s ICS3U course (Grade 11 Introduction to Computer Science, University Preparation, 2008 curriculum), and every lesson is tagged with the expectations it covers.
It isn’t only for Ontario. The lessons suit any similar high school introduction to computer science that’s taught in Python. If you teach elsewhere, use the modules in order, skip the expectation codes, and adapt freely: everything here is MIT licensed.

title: About This Course
text:
The Philosophy

1. Read before you write
Students read code before they write it. Every new idea is first met by reading a short program, predicting what it will do, and tracing it line by line. Writing new code comes last, once students can read it fluently. Every worksheet opens with reading tasks, and every quiz and test includes a code-reading section.


2. Start deep, with real code
Because students read first, they can meet real, interesting programs long before they could write them. The first program students see isn’t “Hello, World”. It asks the computer what kind of processor it has. Students don’t need to understand every line on day one. The parts they can’t yet explain become reasons to keep learning.


3. One new idea at a time
Deep doesn’t mean fast. Lessons start small, often from a single line, and add one piece at a time. Module 1 uses only one library until students are comfortable with it.


4. A spiral, not a list of topics
The course isn’t divided into an output unit, then an input unit, then a decisions unit. Students meet output, input, decisions, loops, strings, and lists early, inside programs they read. Each module comes back to these ideas at a deeper level. Each idea moves through four stages over the course: read it, modify it, write it, then design with it. The spiral table shows where each idea sits in each module.


5. Teacher-led, then gradually independent
Lessons use explicit, direct instruction. The teacher models a worked example, thinking aloud, and students then practise with steadily less support. Each lesson follows the PRIMM sequence: students Predict what code will do, Run it, Investigate how it works, Modify it, and finally Make their own. The course builds toward an independent software project at the end, not from one at the start.

text:
What a Lesson Looks Like







Stage
What happens




Review
Short retrieval questions, often reading or tracing code


Teach
The teacher reads a worked example aloud and traces it


Predict

Students run the code and compare the result with their prediction

title: About This Course
text:
Interactive by Design

Runnable code on every page. Students can edit and run Python right in the lesson page or on the slides, with nothing to install.
Predict, then step. Students type a prediction beside the code, then run the program one line at a time and watch the output and variables appear next to their prediction.
Where does my code run? The same program gives different answers on the classroom computer, in the browser, and on a cloud server. The course uses those differences to teach how computers work.

title: About This Course
text:
Built on Research
This approach draws on research about how novices learn to program:

Students who can’t reliably read and trace code have trouble writing it (Lister et al., 2004; Lopez et al., 2008).
Novices learn more from explicit instruction and worked examples than from open-ended discovery (Sweller & Cooper, 1985; Kirschner, Sweller & Clark, 2006).
Effective lessons review prior learning, present new material in small steps, model, and guide practice before independent work (Rosenshine, 2012).
PRIMM puts reading and predicting ahead of writing in programming lessons (Sentance, Waite & Kallia, 2019).







NoteReferences






Kirschner, P. A., Sweller, J., & Clark, R. E. (2006). Why minimal guidance during instruction does not work. Educational Psychologist, 41(2), 75–86.
Lister, R., et al. (2004). A multi-national study of reading and tracing skills in novice programmers. ITiCSE Working Group Reports, 119–150.
Lopez, M., Whalley, J., Robbins, P., & Lister, R. (2008). Relationships between reading, tracing and writing skills in introductory programming. Proceedings of ICER 2008, 101–112.
Rosenshine, B. (2012). Principles of instruction: Research-based strategies that all teachers should know. American Educator, 36(1), 12–19, 39.
Sentance, S., Waite, J., & Kallia, M. (2019). Teaching computer programming with PRIMM: A sociocultural perspective. Computer Science Education, 29(2–3), 136–176.
Sweller, J., & Cooper, G. A. (1985). The use of worked examples as a substitute for problem solving in learning algebra. Cognition and Instruction, 2(1), 59–89.

text: For students. Covers Lessons 1–2. Work on your classroom computer (Thonny, IDLE, or VS Code). Hand in: your .py file and your answers to Parts A and C.

title: Module 1 Assignment: Computer Report Card
text:
Part A: Read
Read this program without running it, then answer the questions.
import platform

name = platform.node()
cpu = platform.machine()
print("Report card for", name)
print("CPU:", cpu)
cpu = "unknown"
print("Checked:", cpu)

How many lines will it print?
Fill in a trace table (Line, name, cpu, Output) for every line that runs.
What does the last line print? Explain why.
How many times does the program ask the computer for its CPU type?

title: Module 1 Assignment: Computer Report Card
text:
Part B: Write
Write a program called report_card.py that prints a computer report card for the computer it runs on.
Your program must:

Print a title line that includes the computer’s name.
Report at least five facts, using five different platform functions. At least one must be a function you found yourself with dir(platform) or the documentation.
Store each answer in a variable with a clear name before printing it.
Print each fact with a clear label.
Start with a comment giving your name, the date, and what the program does.

Example of the style (your facts and labels will be different):
Report card for LAB-PC-14
CPU type: AMD64
Operating system: Windows
...

title: Module 1 Assignment: Computer Report Card
section: Part C: Run It in Two Places
text:
Part C: Run It in Two Places

Run your program on the classroom computer and copy the output into a comment at the bottom of your file.
Paste the same program into the box below and run it in the browser.








Answer in two or three sentences each:

Which facts were the same in both places? Which were different?
Why are they different? Where did the program actually run each time?
Name one mistake you made while writing the program, and explain how the error message helped you fix it. If you made none, explain what an AttributeError would tell you.

title: Ask the Computer About Itself
text:
Two lines of Python
import platform

print(platform.machine())


import platform brings in a toolbox of ready-made code
platform.machine() asks: what type of CPU is this?
print() shows the answer



Read the program aloud before running it. The dot means “the machine tool from the platform toolbox”; the parentheses mean “use it now”. Then run it on the classroom computer in Thonny, IDLE, or VS Code and compare with the warm-up guesses.

title: Ask the Computer About Itself
text:
What does the answer mean?








Answer
Meaning
Found in




arm64 / aarch64
64-bit ARM
Apple silicon Macs, phones, tablets


x86_64 / AMD64
64-bit Intel or AMD
Most Windows PCs, older Macs, servers




Windows reports Intel and AMD processors as AMD64 because AMD designed the 64-bit version of this processor family.

title: Ask the Computer About Itself
text:
Predict, then run
import platform

print("CPU type:", platform.machine())
print("Operating system:", platform.system())
print("Computer name:", platform.node())

* Why wasm32 and Emscripten? This box runs Python inside your web browser, using Pyodide, so it describes a small virtual computer in this browser tab. Run the program in Thonny, IDLE, or VS Code to see your computer’s real answers.


TEACHER PROMPT (first use of the step-through box): “Nothing has run yet. The red arrow on a yellow line is the NEXT line Python will run. When I press Step, that line runs and turns GREEN — green means just ran. Anything printed appears in Output the moment its line turns green. Back replays a step; Run all jumps to the end; Start over resets.” Then: “Write your prediction first — no pressing Step until you’ve committed.” Ask first: How many lines will it print? Which words appear exactly as written? Which parts depend on the computer? Have students commit to a prediction (type it in the box or write it down), then press Step one line at a time. Afterwards, click once to show the asterisk note explaining the odd answers (wasm32, Emscripten): the box runs Python inside the browser with Pyodide, so it describes a virtual computer in the tab. Then run the same program on the classroom computer and compare.

title: Exploring the platform Library
section: What else is in the toolbox?
text:
What else is in the toolbox?






Python documentation: platform

Skip names starting with an underscore. Point out familiar names (machine, system, node, python_version, release) and new ones (platform, architecture, version, uname). Then open docs.python.org/3/library/platform.html and read the entry for machine() together.

title: Exploring the platform Library
text:
Predict, then step
import platform

cpu = platform.machine()
system = platform.system()
name = platform.node()

print("Computer report for", name)
print("CPU type:", cpu)
print("Operating system:", system)

TEACHER PROMPT (first use of the Variables panel): “Same colours as last lesson. New panel: Variables. A variable is a name that holds a value — watch a row appear when line 3 runs.” After line 3: “Nothing printed, but the answer was stored under the name cpu. The quotation marks around ‘wasm32’ mean the value is text — a string. They won’t be printed.” This is Lesson 1’s report with each answer stored in a variable first. Ask: Which lines ask a question? Which lines print? What will the first line of output be? After predicting, step through and watch the Variables panel: lines 3–5 print nothing, but the variables appear.

title: Exploring the platform Library
text:
What the variables hold

After line 3, which variable exists? What is its value?
Lines 3–5 print nothing. Where did the answers go?
What if line 7 came before line 5?


Quotation marks in the Variables panel (e.g. ‘wasm32’) show the value is text (a string); they are not printed.

title: Exploring the platform Library
text:
Spot the problem: A
import platform

print(platform.machine)

No parentheses, so Python prints the tool itself, not its answer.

title: Exploring the platform Library
text:
Spot the problem: B
import platform

print(platform.cpu())
